reconcile.connective: Commentators resolve the tension by distinguishing the objects: Hebrews and John commend faith in revealed divine realities, while Colossians condemns self-invented visions of angels as fleshly presumption.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells (Skeptic's Annotated Bible) flags the surface tension: Hebrews praises belief in the unseen while Colossians condemns it, and the object-distinction harmonization depends on a theological classification the texts themselves do not articulate.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text:
intruding into those things which he hath not seen; thrusting himself in a bold and daring manner into an inquiry and search after, debate upon, and affirmation of things he could have no certain knowledge of; as of angels, whose nature, qualities, works, and ministrations, he had never seen with his bodily eyes; nor could ever discern with the eyes of his understanding any such things in the Scriptures, which he ascribed to them; but they were the birth of his own mind, the fruits of his own fancy and imagination, things devised in his own brain: being
vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind; judging of things not according to the word of God, and with a spiritual judgment, and according to a spiritual sense and experience, but according to his own carnal reason, and the vanity of his mind
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill distinguishes the Colossians condemnation from commended faith: the problem is self-invented, carnally-reasoned speculation about angels — not the scripturally-grounded faith in unseen divine realities that Hebrews and John 20:29 commend. This directly addresses the apparent contradiction.

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Faith without sight, in other respects, may be considered as opposed to the beatific vision in heaven; and as destitute of sensible communion with God; and as giving credit to doctrines and things above carnal sense and reason; such as the doctrines of the Trinity, the sonship of Christ, his incarnation, and the union of the two natures in him, and the resurrection of the dead; and as believing whatever is said in the word of God, upon the credit of his testimony
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill defines commended 'belief in the unseen' as trust in Scripture's revealed testimony about divine realities — a categorically different act from the angel-speculation Colossians condemns, directly resolving the tension.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley addresses apparent contradictions between commended faith and condemned speculation, applying the standard harmonization that the objects and grounds of belief differ between the passages.
